chapter_theme: Pranayama (பிராணாயாமம்): the breath is a horse that throws the false and carries the true, mastered only by the guru's grace; held with the mind and measured in inhaling, holding and exhaling, it stops birth and death, keeps the body young, keeps Siva within and kicks away Death.
structure_note: Images of the breath as a horse (564 to 566), the claim for breath held with the mind (567), the measures of puraka, kumbhaka and recaka (568, 570 to 574), the fruits in the body (569, 575), and two riddles of the twelve finger-breadths (576, 577).

564.reading: The lord of the five, chief of that town, has another horse to ride to salvation; it gives a hold to the true but leaps and throws the false.
564.nuance: The horse is traditionally the breath, the five the senses and the town the body, with the soul as their lord; none of this is named. மெய்யர் and பொய்யர் may be the truthful and the false, or those firm and unfirm in practice.

565.reading: There are two horses, though one is no noble rider, and none knows the skill to cast and catch them; if one gains the grace of the keen lord, the guru, they come under control.
565.nuance: The two horses are traditionally the breaths of the left and right nostril (ida and pingala). ஆரியன் அல்லன் is obscure: it may say the rider is not skilled, or that no master is at hand.

566.reading: If you ride the horse swifter than a bird, it gives intoxication without drinking toddy, makes one move lightly and drives off sloth; we have told the truth to those who understand.
566.nuance: Toddy (கள்) stands for a joy that needs nothing outside the body. The horse is the controlled breath, as in 564; the last line marks the teaching as for the prepared.

567.reading: If the breath stays with the mind without moving, there is no birth or death; the breath, turned in its channel, makes speech known, and you have gained the gift of the breath.
567.nuance: மடைமாறி (changing course, as water at a sluice) and பேச்சறிவித்து are unclear: the line may mean the breath turned within gives knowledge of the inner sound or of mantra. The first two lines are the plain claim.

568.reading: Drawing in is puraka, sixteen measures by the left; holding is kumbhaka, sixty-four; letting out is recaka, thirty-two; to change the order in one of these is deceit.
568.nuance: The ratio 16:64:32 is the standard one. வஞ்சகம் in the last line is unclear: it may condemn changing the measures, or name the alternation of nostrils as the 'clever' method.

569.reading: If one draws in the air and holds it under control, a ripened body becomes unripe and clear as crystal; if one clearly gains the guru's grace, one becomes swifter than the wind.
569.nuance: பழுக்கினும் பிஞ்சாம் (though ripe, it becomes unripe) promises a return to youth. வளியினும் வேட்டு வளியனும் is obscure; it may mean master of the wind. The variant வயிற்றில் (in the belly) places the holding in the abdomen.

570.reading: Wherever you are, fill the breath on the left; doing it there, the body does not decay; holding it there and releasing it in measure, one becomes master as the conch signals.
570.nuance: இடம் may be 'the left' or 'the place'. சங்கே குறிக்க is unclear: the conch may be an inner sound heard in practice, or a sign of the master.

571.reading: No one knows the measure of holding the breath that one draws in and lets out through both nostrils; for those who know it, it is the means to kick Death.
571.nuance: இருகால் may mean the two breaths or the two nostrils. Kicking Death (கூற்றை உதைக்கும்) echoes the story of Siva kicking Death for Markandeya; whether the verse promises a long life or release from death is left open.

572.reading: Filling the breath fully above, below, in the middle and at the sides, settling it within by recaka, and holding it in the navel, one may gain the grace of the one who drank the poison.
572.nuance: ஆலாலம் உண்டான் is Siva, who drank the halahala poison. பாலாம் இரேசகம் and மாலாகி are unclear: மால் may mean fullness, delight or Vishnu.

573.reading: Fill sixteen measures through the left, let out thirty-two gladly with pingala as the eye, and hold sixty-four between the two: this is the truth.
573.nuance: It repeats the measures of 568 and adds that exhaling is through pingala, the right channel. ஓமத்தால் is unclear: it may mean 'in between' or 'as an offering'.

574.reading: Without loosening the seat one has set, breathe out, fill all ten nadis, and hold prana and apana together; if one stays still, there is no Yama for us.
574.nuance: இட்ட அவ்வீடு (that house one set) may be the posture or the body. நட்டம் may mean steadiness or dance. நமனில்லை (no Yama) can be read as long life or as freedom from death.

575.reading: If the breath that wanders out and in is guided within and made pure, the limbs grow ruddy, the hair turns black, and the one with matted locks will not leave.
575.nuance: The bodily signs are stated plainly: ruddy limbs and black hair, the marks of youth. புரிசடையோன் is Siva; the verse puts him in the purified body. The same last line returns in 586.

576.reading: The women who built a house and moved in run out and come back twelve finger-breadths; they reach out eight fingers and cut back four; if gathered in, they become the five letters.
576.nuance: The women are traditionally the breaths and the house the body; the breath goes out twelve finger-breadths, eight return and four are lost. அஞ்செழுத்து is the five-syllable mantra of Siva, so the held breath becomes mantra. All of this rests on a symbolic reading.

577.reading: Twelve elephants have day and night; the mahout does not know them; once the mahout knows the twelve elephants, they have no day and night.
577.nuance: The twelve are traditionally the twelve finger-breadths of the breath (as in 576), the mahout the soul, and day and night the right and left breaths (sun and moon). Once the breath is known it no longer alternates. The riddle has other readings, such as the twelve signs.

links.note: Both say a discipline can overcome Death (கூற்று): the Kural credits the power of tapas with leaping past Death, Tirumular the measure of the held breath with kicking him.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood because grey hair will surely come; Tirumular says purified breath turns the hair black. Read literally, they disagree about whether ageing can be undone; read symbolically, 575 is not about hair, and the tension dissolves.
Both turn on twelve: 576 says the breath goes out twelve finger-breadths, and 577 makes the twelve elephants that, once known, no longer keep day and night.

564 says the horse of the breath gives a hold to the true but leaps and throws the false (துள்ளி விழுத்திடும்); Kural 814 says better solitude than friends like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle (அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா). The thrown rider figures false friendship in the Kural and unfit practice in the Tirumanthiram.

565 says the two horses of the breath come under control only with the guru's grace (குருவின் அருள்பெற்றால் ... வசப்படும்); 1679 says hold the reins of the running horse firmly (ஓடுங் குதிரைக்கு உசை திண்ணம் பற்றுமின்) and seek Nandi rather than put on a garb. Both make the restless horse the thing to master, and both send the learner to the Lord or guru rather than outward forms.

335 sets yogis who bind the breath and taste the nectar of knowledge-bliss against the deluded who drink liquor and lose their understanding; 566 says the horse of the breath gives intoxication without drinking toddy (கள்ளுண்ண வேண்டாந் தானே களிதரும்). 566 states as a promise the joy that 335 sets against drink.

566 says the controlled breath gives elation without toddy (கள்ளுண்ண வேண்டா ... களிதரும்); Kural 1090 says brewed liquor delights only those who drink it, unlike love, which delights by a look (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது அடுநறா). The same comparison, a joy that surpasses liquor because it needs no drinking, is made of love in the Kural and of breath in the Tirumanthiram.

A near-repeat: 568 gives the measures of breath as sixteen in, sixty-four held and thirty-two out (ஈரெட்டு ... அறுபத்து நாலு ... முப்பத்திரண்டு); 573 repeats the same sixteen, thirty-two and sixty-four (ஈரெட்டு ... முப்பத்திரண்டு ... எட்டெட்டு) and adds that the exhalation goes by pingala.

569 says if one draws in the air and holds it, the ripened body becomes unripe (பழுக்கினும் பிஞ்சாம்); 722 says if one ties fast the horse of twelve legs, the body will not leave for thousands of years (பேராது காயம்). Both promise that the held breath keeps the body from ageing.

577 figures the breath as twelve elephants (பன்னிரண்டானை) the mahout must come to know; 722 figures it as a horse with twelve legs (ஈராறு கால்) to be tied fast. The same count of twelve, the breath's finger-breadths on the traditional reading, gives the beast its form in both.

source_issues: 569: a variant reads வயிற்றில் (in the belly) for வயத்தில் (under control), which changes where the breath is held.
567: a variant reads தடக்கிப் for தடங்கிப்; the sense is close.
568: a variant reads கும்பகம் for கும்பம்; the sense is the same.
